newsitem.title: USA: Airline workers press for share of soaring profits.
newsitem.headline: Airline workers press for share of soaring profits.

text.p: Employees who not so long ago gave up raises to keep their struggling airlines aloft are looking to make up for lost time now that profits are soaring.

At two major carriers, American Airlines and United Airlines, rank and file union members recently rebelled against contract settlements recommended by their leaders and demanded that they go back to the bargaining table for more.
"Unions know it's a cyclical business," said Larry Crawford of Avitas Aviation Inc., a Reston, Va., aviation consultant. "Obviously, the time to ask for more is in the good times."

"That's always been the way with airlines," said Crawford, who predicted that union demands for a share of the growing profits would lead to some strikes. "Management takes advantage in downtimes and gives up that advantage in the uptimes."
For the airlines, the skies couldn't be friendlier.
Net profits at the 12 top U.S. carriers climbed to a record $1.2 billion in the third quarter, despite higher fuel prices, the Transportation Department reported last week.

Perhaps the most contentious situation is at American Airlines, where more than 60 percent of the 8,600 pilots last week rejected their union's recommendation to accept a contract that would have raised pay by 5 percent over four years.
Leaders of the union, the independent Allied Pilots Association, have since expanded their list of bargaining demands and raised the possibility of a strike.
The airline, which is owned by Fort Worth, Texas-based AMR Corp., said on Friday it would accept arbitration to resolve the dispute, but the union has said it would not.

If arbitration is rejected and further talks seem fruitless, the federal National Mediation Board could declare an impasse that would start a 30-day countdown after which the union could strike or the airline could implement its offer.
Hanging in the balance is American's plan to buy 103 new planes from Boeing Co. and take out options to buy 527 more, if the pilots had approved the contract.
Airline analyst Glenn Engel of Goldman Sachs & Co. said a strike by American's pilots was unlikely since they are already among the highest paid in the industry.
"I would be surprised if American has a work stoppage," he said. "It's in nobody's interest for there to be a strike."

Higher profits and tighter labor markets -- in sharp contrast to the industry's lean years of the early 1990s -- are giving union workers the leverage to demand more from the airline industry, even though most are already cashing on the bonanza through profit-sharing schemes, Engle said.
"Labor wants to have its cake and eat it too," he said, adding that airline labor costs rose 5 percent to 6 percent in 1996.
But unions see the current good times as an opportunity to get back cash and rights they gave up during the hard times.

"It's better than it's been in a long time and the people who made concessions in years back are looking for some payback," said Bob Flocke of the Air Line Pilots Association, which represents 43,000 pilots at 38 domestic airlines.

At United Airlines, many of the carrier's 8,500 pilots are campaigning against accepting a package that would raise pay by more than 10 percent over four years. ALPA is scheduled to announce the results of the vote on Friday.

United, owned by Chicago-based UAL Corp., was the scene of another insurrection by more than 12,000 mechanics represented by the International Association of Machinists, who last week rejected an identical pay proposal.
But roughly as many IAM-represented ramp, dispatch, food service and other workers at United accepted the deal.
Pay disputes at United, where all major employee groups except the flight attendants took part in a 1994 employee buyout, are submitted to arbitration to avoid strikes.
The Association of Flight Attendants also is negotiating with United, but the talks have been sidetracked.

"We're sitting here watching a company boast about being one of the most profitable companies in the world, which just begs the question, what about sharing it with your workers?" said AFA spokeswoman Jane Goodman.

While union officials said there are no common goals in bargaining, especially at smaller airlines, they said the mood among employees at other larger carriers was also to resist concessions and recoup lost raises of the past.

St. Paul, Minn.-based Northwest Airlines Corp. is negotiating with all of its unions, while USAir Group Inc. of Arlington, Va., is reportedly asking ALPA for a concessionary package that would create a new low-cost unit, with salaries to match, to compete with its discount rivals.
Negotiations are expected to begin in July between ALPA and Houston-based Continental Airlines Inc. and in September between Trans World Airlines Inc. and its unions.
